1.pericope_label: And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Cesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed. (And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.) And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city. And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:) To be taxed with Mary his espoused wife, being great with child.

schools.summary: Barnes would render "all the world" the whole land, meaning Palestine, since no ancient writer mentions such a taxing and Luke's account demands no more; on Cyrenius he follows Lardner in making this the first census of the man afterwards familiarly known as governor, defending the idiom by observing that one may say General Washington saved Braddock's army. Ellicott keeps the Roman empire and answers the historians' silence from the policy of Augustus, who took such returns about every ten years and laid a survey of the empire before the Senate; he refuses the reading that turns "first" into "before", the construction being absent from Luke elsewhere and unnatural across twelve years, supplies a missing governor from a coin of Antioch, shows Quirinus already in office in the East, and emphasises the adjective, that this enrolment was the first under his government. Robertson insists it was a census and not a taxing and appeals to Ramsay for a fourteen-year census cycle in Egypt and inscriptions proving Quirinus twice in Syria. Lightfoot sets out Dion Cassius on the date and then declines the question: let the more learned judge.

Henry reads the date as the proof of the hour, the fourth monarchy at its height, Judea become a province and taxed with the rest, and the temple of Janus shut, so that the sceptre had departed from Judah and Shiloh must come.

Calvin sets human contrivance aside, since Joseph and Mary had no design but to obey the edict and were led like blind persons by the hand of God to the place where Christ must be born; he presses the irony twice, that an ungodly man seizes what God was accustomed to demand of his people, and that the officer executing Caesar's commission is, unknown to himself, God's herald calling Mary to Bethlehem. On the chronology he suspects Josephus's recollection simply failed him, and adds that the edict may have been delayed by tumult, Coponius being sent with an army.

Clarke agrees the Romans had no right to levy where their dominion did not reach, shows from Polybius and Plutarch that the word was used of the Roman government, and restrains it to Judea as the Septuagint does; on Cyrenius he offers Lardner's solution and a second, that the word rendered first may mean before, as where John says he was before me, and prefers the second.

Bede makes the peace itself the sign, there being no greater token of it than the whole world brought under one taxing, and hears a literal fulfilment of the swords beaten into ploughshares. Ambrose finds a secular registration implying a spiritual, a census of souls laid before the King not of earth but of heaven, the old census of the Synagogue abolished and a new one of the Church preparing; he asks who could demand the registering of the whole world but the one whose the earth is, and notes that the just man and the virgin came up to it, he who kept the word and she who obeyed it. Gregory calls the registering mystical, since he appeared in the flesh who should write down the names of his own elect in eternity. Leo turns it to the hearer: there is one common measure of joy, so the saint may exult, the sinner be glad, the gentile take courage.
Origen sees a kind of sacrament in it: Christ's name being written with all, he might sanctify all.
Theophylact adds that one king rules the world because at Christ's coming the worship of many gods should cease.

positions.view: The whole land, that is Palestine; no ancient writer mentions a universal taxing
The inhabited part under Roman dominion, restrained here to Judea as the Septuagint restrains it
The Roman empire, as throughout the New Testament; the historians' silence is answered from the policy of Augustus

debates.question: How can the enrolment be dated by a governor who held Syria twelve years later?

positions.view: It was the first census of the man afterwards familiarly known as governor
The word rendered "first" means "before", as in John's "he was before me"
No; emphasise the adjective instead, Quirinus having already held office in the East, a missing governor being supplied from a coin of Antioch
Ramsay's fourteen-year census cycle and inscriptions showing Quirinus twice in Syria settle it
Josephus's recollection failed him, and the edict may have been delayed by tumult
Undecided: let the more learned judge

outliers.claim: Makes the census itself the point rather than its date, reading a secular registration as implying a spiritual one, with the old census of the Synagogue abolished and a new census of the Church preparing.

themes: And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Cesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed.
(And this taxing was first made when Cyrenius was governor of Syria.)
And all went to be taxed, every one into his own city.
And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:)

6.pericope_label: And so it was, that, while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered. And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.

schools.summary: Jerome answers Helvidius on the word firstborn by distinguishing: every only-begotten is firstborn but not every firstborn only-begotten, the firstborn being not he whom others follow but he before whom there is none. Bede divides the title instead, only-begotten in the substance of divinity, firstborn in the taking of humanity, firstborn in grace and only-begotten in nature; and he sets out the swaddling and the manger as a series of exchanges, since he who clothes the whole world with its varied beauty is wrapped in common linen that we might receive the best robe, is folded hand and foot that our hands might be raised to good work, and finds no room in an inn though he sits at the Father's right hand, that he might prepare many mansions.

Gregory of Nyssa holds the birth not wholly subject to the laws of our nature, the burden light and the delivery without pain, since she who engrafted death was condemned to bring forth in trouble and she who brought life should be delivered with joy. Chrysostom adds that he might have come moving the heavens and shooting thunderbolts, but his desire was to save and to trample on human pride from its birth. The Greek Exposition wonders at the straitening undergone by one who holds the world in his hands, and finds him seeking poverty from the beginning and ennobling it in himself.
Cyril makes the manger the place of food, that men grown like the beasts might partake not of hay but of heavenly bread.

Barnes explains that the word rendered inn means only a halting place, a khan or caravanserai, puts Joseph and Mary in one of the recesses off the stable down to the unfurnished cells and the cloth stretched across for privacy, says plainly that the obvious meaning of firstborn is that Mary had other children, and takes the middle way on poverty, that being there proved nothing but necessity while Jesus was nevertheless born poor and cradled in no palace. Robertson agrees on firstborn that there is not a particle of evidence for the contrary notion. Ellicott reports the tradition of a cave, which Justin Martyr read as fulfilling a prophecy of a place of defence in a lofty rock, notes that limestone caves were commonly used as stables, traces the ox and the ass of the paintings to a fanciful reading of Isaiah, and identifies the inn as the lodging of Chimham, built by the son of Barzillai. Lightfoot reports with Gill the Arabian who told a Jew the Redeemer was born, naming Menahem son of Hezekiah at Birath Arba, and being unable to say what the place was decides a man had better hold his tongue than conjecture to no purpose.

Calvin sees both the great poverty of Joseph and a tyranny which compelled him to bring his wife at so inconvenient a season, supposes the royal line was handled the more harshly, and has Joseph, unable to avoid it, bow his head and commend himself to God. Gill joins Lightfoot in reporting the rabbinic tradition of the Arabian and the Jew.

Clarke shows from Wetstein that the word means not the crib but the whole stable, quotes Virgil on horses standing in lofty stables, and objects outright to the argument from poverty: the reason given is that there was no room, an honest man blessed in his business could not have been unable to procure a night's lodging, and he would not have brought his wife at all had he been so ill fitted for the journey. Wesley only remarks that now also there is seldom room for Christ in an inn.
Henry counts the stable an instance of his parents' poverty and of the manners of the age, since men with any common humanity would not have turned a woman in travail into a stable.

debates.question: Does the word "firstborn" imply that Mary had other children?

positions.view: No; every only-begotten is firstborn, and the firstborn is he before whom there is none
The title divides instead, only-begotten in divinity and firstborn in humanity
Yes; that is the obvious meaning, and there is not a particle of evidence for the contrary

debates.question: Does the manger prove the family poor?

positions.view: Yes, and a cruel tyranny besides, which compelled Joseph to bring his wife at such a season
Yes, and it indicts the manners of the age as well
No; the reason given is that there was no room, and an honest working man could have afforded a night's lodging
Being there proved only necessity, though Jesus was nevertheless born poor

outliers.claim: Prefers the cave tradition to the stable, citing Justin Martyr's appeal to a prophecy of a place of defence in a lofty rock, and traces the ox and the ass of Christian art to a fanciful reading of Isaiah rather than to the narrative.

themes: And so it was, that, while they were there, the days were accomplished that she should be delivered.
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn.

8.pericope_label: And there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night. And, lo, the angel of the Lord came upon them, and the glory of the Lord shone round about them: and they were sore afraid. And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Saviour, which is Christ the Lord. And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.

schools.summary: Chrysostom observes that the angel came to Joseph in a dream, as to one easily brought to believe, and to the shepherds in visible shape, as to men of a ruder nature, and that he sought no scribes, who were tormented with envy, there being a road which leads by innocence to philosophy; on the hymn he sets the change against the old errands, when angels were sent to punish Israel and David and Sodom, where now they sing thanksgiving, God having brought angels down to men and men up to heaven. The Greek Exposition refers Saviour to the action and Lord to the dignity of the person, and observes that the angel not only soothes terror but pours in gladness.

Bede notes that nowhere in the Old Testament do angels appear by day, the privilege being kept for the hour when a light arose in the darkness, and sets the sides together: he is sent forth from the womb but shines from heaven, lies in a common inn but lives in celestial light. He marks what the sign was, not Tyrian purple and a gilded couch but poor swaddling clothes and a manger, explains the multitude by saying a single angel's authority might have seemed small, and hears the host wishing peace to men once despised as abject and now esteemed as friends. Gregory finds the watching rewarded, since those see sublime things who watch over their flocks.

Cyril takes the middle of the three names as the ground of adoration, signifying not the nature but the compound substance of two natures, and distinguishes the anointing from the figurative kind poured on kings, or on Cyrus the idolater. Origen raises the objection that the Lord says he came not to send peace on earth, and answers that the peace withheld is not the peace of good will.

Lightfoot identifies the flocks as the sheep of the wilderness, driven out about the Passover and brought home at the first rain in Marchesvan, and on the hymn takes "good will toward men" for the subject and the rest for the predicate, so that good will is glory to God in the highest and peace on earth. Ellicott takes the season just before the Passover, when the grass is greenest, notes that the traditional date appears only in the fourth century and may have been chosen to displace the Saturnalia, and adds from the Mishna that the temple's sacrificial sheep were pastured in these fields, so that men lately rejoicing over the Paschal lambs heard now of the Lamb of God; with Robertson he prefers the genitive of the oldest manuscripts, peace among men of good will, refuses the softer rendering, and notes that the clause has no verb and may be read as proclamation or prayer. Barnes agrees the birth was probably earlier than December, then stops: what God regards as unimportant he conceals.

Clarke concludes that the nativity in December should on this ground be given up, and reports from Fabricius a hundred and thirty-six opinions about the year, the day having been placed in every month, until Pope Julius fixed on the twenty-fifth, which the Romans kept as the feast of Bruma.
Henry adds that the chief priests were not prepared for the tidings, and that the shepherds were neither asleep nor at their devotions but at their calling.

Calvin grants the method looks unsuitable and makes that the point, the treasure being deposited in earthen vessels, so that we should not be ashamed of instructors taken from among the dung of cattle; and he presses the pronoun, since it would give no delight to hear the Author of salvation is born unless each believed he was born for him.

positions.view: Not in December; the flocks in the open are a chronological fact, and the twenty-fifth was fixed by Pope Julius on the day of the feast of Bruma
Just before the Passover, when the grass is greenest; the traditional date appears only in the fourth century
Probably earlier than December, but the time is unknown and God conceals what he regards as unimportant
The day's greatness is itself doubtful, the sacrifices diminishing through the week

debates.question: Is it "peace, good will toward men" or "peace among men of good will"?

positions.view: The genitive of the oldest manuscripts: peace among men who are the objects of God's approval
Take good will toward men as the subject and the rest as predicate, so that God's good will is both the glory and the peace

outliers.claim: Explains the choice of shepherds over scribes by their character rather than their rank, holding that the learned were disqualified by envy and that there is a road which leads by innocence to philosophy.

And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger.

Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.

15.pericope_label: And it came to pass, as the angels were gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said one to another, Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass, which the Lord hath made known unto us. And they came with haste, and found Mary, and Joseph, and the babe lying in a manger. And when they had seen it, they made known abroad the saying which was told them concerning this child. And all they that heard it wondered at those things which were told them by the shepherds. But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart. And the shepherds returned, glorifying and praising God for all the things that they had heard and seen, as it was told unto them.

schools.summary: Bede fastens on what the shepherds said, that they would see not the child but the word which had come to pass, so the errand is to see how the Word was made flesh; he says the shepherds of the Church were ordained to this end, that what they learn in the Scriptures they explain to their hearers, extends the office to every private man who rules his good actions with due moderation, and keeps Mary to the laws of virgin modesty, divulging the secrets of Christ to none but comparing what she had read in prophecy with what she now saw. Ambrose remarks how exactly Scripture weighs each term, since in beholding the flesh of the Lord we behold the Word, warns that their humble character makes this no slight example of faith, simplicity being sought and not pride, adds that no one indolently seeks after Christ, and bids us learn the chastity of the Virgin, no less chaste in her words than in her body. The Gloss marvels at the attestation itself, by men who could not have devised such things but were proclaiming truth with simple eloquence.

The Greek Exposition has them leave the sheepfolds and set out by night after the Saviour's light, and collects Mary's whole store, whatever the angel had said and whatever she heard from Zacharias and Elisabeth and the shepherds, finding that on comparison she perceived one harmony.

Origen reads the three they found as the mother who brought Jesus into the world, the guardian of the birth, and the Saviour himself, and calls it the manger Israel knew not, where the ox knows his owner.

Calvin notes that they were never expressly commanded to go and went because they knew God's design, draws the lesson that the word must not pass away with the sound, and observes that they exhort one another, since it is not enough that each attend to his own duty. He calls the sight at Bethlehem revolting and enough of itself to produce aversion, nothing being less probable than that the King of the whole people should be one unworthy to rank with the lowest, yet the glory of God was so before their eyes that their faith rose above everything mean in Christ; he agrees their low rank diminished their credit, and observes that though all were astonished not one moved a step, so the report left the people's ignorance inexcusable. On the return he adds that if the cradle raised these men from the stable to heaven, how much more should the death and resurrection raise us.

Ellicott grants the adoration is implied though not stated, and assigns the ox and the ass of the pictures, with the light glowing from the cradle, to the apocryphal legends. Barnes says they now had evidence that would satisfy others and makes it a duty of the newly converted to tell what they have seen and felt, and calls the pondering a delicate expression of a mother's feelings. Robertson keeps the imperfect, a keeping together that did not stop, and wonders whether Mary kept a baby book that Luke may have seen.

Clarke asks what the shepherds' text was and answers from the hymn, glory to God and peace and good will among men, then turns it against the crusades and against wars for religion as an insult to the gospel; on the pondering he takes the word for weighing in its Latin sense, each new circumstance measured against those past.
Henry adds that the truths of Christ are worth keeping and the way to keep them safe is to ponder them, meditation being the best help to memory.

debates.question: What did the shepherds propose to see?

positions.view: Not the child but the word which had come to pass, that is, how the Word was made flesh
The Saviour's light, after which they left the sheepfolds and set out by night

debates.question: Are the ox and the ass of the pictures part of the narrative?

positions.view: No; they belong to the apocryphal legends alone
The manger is the one Israel knew not, where the ox knows his owner

outliers.claim: Turns the shepherds' message into a polemic, making the hymn the whole substance of the gospel and condemning the crusades and all wars for the support of religion as an insult to it.

21.pericope_label: And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb. And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord; (As it is written in the law of the Lord, Every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord;) And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.

schools.summary: Epiphanius gives four reasons for the circumcision, to show the reality of the flesh against those who said he came in appearance only, to prove the body not of one substance with the Deity nor descended from heaven as Valentinian said, to confirm a rite he had himself instituted, and to leave the Jews no excuse for refusing an uncircumcised Christ; against Ebion and Cerinthus, who argued that disciples must therefore be circumcised, he turns their premise, that if Christ is mere man a boy can no more cause his own circumcision than any infant. Gregory of Nyssa finds the law of the opened womb peculiarly fulfilled, since he alone opened a womb till then unopened and left its seal after the birth. Titus of Bostra holds that Mary, having conceived of the Holy Spirit, was free from all uncleanness.

Origen answers the Ebionites that as we died and rose with him so with him were we circumcised, and need none in the flesh. Cyril ties the day to the rising, since on the eighth day Christ rose and conveyed a spiritual circumcision, the name being imposed on the same day.

Bede makes the circumcision an example of obedience and a compassion on men unable to bear the law, circumcision having brought to original sin the cure baptism brings now, save that the circumcised waited in a blessed rest outside the kingdom; he finds the precedent for the naming in Abraham, who on the day of his circumcision was thought worthy of an increase of his name, and carries it to the elect, that as from Christ they are called Christians so from the Saviour they may be called saved. On the offering he gives several keys, the pigeon for simplicity and the turtle dove for chastity, since having lost her mate she heeds not to find another, or the turtle solitary and the pigeon in flocks, one pointing to the secret tears of confession and the other to the public assembling of the Church, or one to the contemplative and the other to the active life; and Luke, he observes, purposely omits which was offered, so as not to prefer one life before the other. He also finds Mary exempt from the law, since not every woman who brings forth but she who has received seed is pronounced unclean, so that she submitted of her own will.

Henry presses the legal force of the act, that by it he made himself a debtor to the whole law, circumcision being, as Doctor Goodwin says, the bond by which we acknowledged ourselves debtors, to which Christ set his hand; and he argues that a circumcision at eight days makes far more for dedicating the infant seed of the church than a baptism at thirty makes for deferring it.

Calvin refuses to read the purification law as merely political, holding it set before the Jews the corruption of their nature and proves original sin of itself, since the Lord declares the child comes from its mother polluted, and that the fountain of purity chose to be reckoned unclean to wash away our stains; on the offering he meets the objection from the Magi's gold by answering that we do not read of camels laden with it.

Clarke makes the obedience practical: had Mary not kept the days she could not have appeared in public worship and would have passed for an apostate, and uncircumcised he would have had no Jewish hearers; he takes the substitution of the doves as proof that the family was not in affluence.

Ellicott grants that neither rite was here necessary and explains the act as simple obedience, the mystery of the birth not yet being revealed to Mary, and reads the doves as another indication of poverty. Lightfoot reports that this was the offering of the poor, which a rich man offering did not do his duty, and that King Agrippa, coming with a thousand burnt offerings, was prevented by a poor man with two turtledoves.

positions.view: For four reasons: the reality of the flesh, the body's distinct substance, the confirmation of his own rite, and to leave the Jews no excuse
As an example of obedience and a compassion on men unable to bear the law
To convey a spiritual circumcision, the eighth day being the day of the rising
As the bond by which he made himself debtor to the whole law, which also commends infant dedication
No; the law pronounces unclean only she who has received seed, so she submitted of her own will
The law proves original sin and is no mere civil rule; the fountain of purity chose to be reckoned unclean
Neither rite was necessary; the act was simple obedience, the mystery not yet revealed to her
Without it she could not have appeared in public worship and would have passed for an apostate

outliers.claim: Turns the eighth-day circumcision into an argument for infant baptism, holding that it makes far more for dedicating the church's infant seed than Christ's baptism at thirty makes for deferring it.

themes: And when eight days were accomplished for the circumcising of the child, his name was called JESUS, which was so named of the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
And when the days of her purification according to the law of Moses were accomplished, they brought him to Jerusalem, to present him to the Lord;
(As it is written in the law of the Lord, Every male that openeth the womb shall be called holy to the Lord;)
And to offer a sacrifice according to that which is said in the law of the Lord, A pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.

25.pericope_label: And, behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon; and the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him. And it was revealed unto him by the Holy Ghost, that he should not see death, before he had seen the Lord’s Christ. And he came by the Spirit into the temple: and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him after the custom of the law, Then took he him up in his arms, and blessed God, and said, Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation, Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people; A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.

schools.summary: Clarke reports that several learned men make Simeon Hillel's son and president of the grand Sanhedrin. Ellicott develops it, naming him the father of Gamaliel, and finds it suggestive that the Mishna passes his name over as though he stood under a cloud for believing in the prophet of Nazareth, but sets against it that Luke's manner implies a man of very advanced age awaiting his departure, and concludes that the name was so common that all conjectures are precarious; with Robertson he presses the words for Lord and for departing, which belong to the manumission of a slave, so that Simeon speaks as one set free, after weary years on the watch-tower of expectation, by the rising sun. Lightfoot clears away the Simeon the Just of the Jewish histories, grants that Rabban Simeon the son of Hillel was living at Jerusalem in those years, and remarks that nothing is recited from him in the Mishna, which he calls very extraordinary and cannot explain. Barnes allows only that nothing is certainly known of him.

Ambrose observes that righteousness is scarcely preserved without fear, not the fear that dreads the loss of worldly goods, which perfect love casts out, but the holy fear by which a man grows the more careful not to offend as his love grows ardent. Bede makes the exchange at the taking in the arms visible, the righteous man under the law receiving the infant to signify that the righteousness of works was to give place to the lowly but saving grace of faith, and the old man receiving the child to show that a world worn with age should return to childlike innocence; and he notes that the enlightening of the Gentiles is rightly set before the glory of Israel, because when their fullness has come in then shall Israel be safe.

Gregory of Nyssa denies that what Simeon awaited was worldly happiness, taking it for a passing over to the beauty of truth from the shadow of the law; he calls blessed the eyes of his soul and body alike, and marks the widening, since a man waiting for the consolation of Israel cries out on obtaining it that he has seen the salvation of all people. Theophylact hears in the address an acknowledgement that the child in those arms is Lord of life and death, and so God. Basil adds that if you examine the words of the righteous you find them all sorrowing over this world and its mournful delay. The Greek Exposition notes the promise fulfilled, since he was to see the Lord's Christ before he saw death, and now neither dismay at its taste nor doubting thoughts remain.

Origen bids a man who would hold Jesus have the Spirit for guide and come to the temple, and puts Simeon's release in those hands: as long as he held not Christ he was in prison. Cyril keeps the paradox plain, that the Legislator is subject to his own decrees and paid the half shekel though as Son he owed no tax, so a man who sees him keeping the law should not be offended but reflect on the plan of salvation.

Calvin makes the narrative a doctrine of the remnant, since nearly the whole nation was profane and within this small band lay the Church of God while the priests and scribes claimed the title, all having the Messiah's name on their lips but hardly one enduring present affliction in the assurance that redemption was at hand; he allows Simeon may have been of humble rank and no reputation, and warns against those who plead this example and boast they would die willingly if this or that were granted first, since Simeon had a promise and they have only their wishes.

positions.view: The son of Hillel, president of the grand Sanhedrin
The son of Hillel and father of Gamaliel, whom the Mishna passes over as under a cloud; but the age tells against it and all conjectures are precarious
Not Simeon the Just; Rabban Simeon son of Hillel was living then, but nothing is recited from him, which is very extraordinary
Nothing is certainly known; he may have been of humble rank and no reputation

outliers.claim: Generalises Simeon's longing into a mark of all the righteous, who are found on examination to sorrow over this world and its mournful delay.

themes: And, behold, there was a man in Jerusalem, whose name was Simeon; and the same man was just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him.
And it was revealed unto him by the Holy Ghost, that he should not see death, before he had seen the Lord’s Christ.
And he came by the Spirit into the temple: and when the parents brought in the child Jesus, to do for him after the custom of the law,
Then took he him up in his arms, and blessed God, and said,
Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word:
For mine eyes have seen thy salvation,
Which thou hast prepared before the face of all people;
A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel.

33.pericope_label: And Joseph and his mother marvelled at those things which were spoken of him. And Simeon blessed them, and said unto Mary his mother, Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against; (Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.

schools.summary: Bede explains the title of father, held not because Joseph was the real one, as the Photinians say, but because out of regard for Mary all men took him so; on the sword he refuses the reading of martyrdom, since no history tells of her being slain and iron kills the body and not the soul, so that it must be the grief of the passion, which she could not watch unmoved even while certain he would overcome death. Ambrose takes the sword instead for the word of God, sharper than the sharpest, and so a proof of her wisdom.

The Greek Exposition notes that Simeon blessed them both but gave the presage only to the mother, so as neither to strip Joseph of the likeness of a father nor leave her unnamed as the true one. Gregory of Nyssa distinguishes salvation, prepared before the face of all people, from the falling and raising, which is of many, and applies the fall chiefly to Israel, who must forfeit ancient privileges for refusing one who had come forth from them; on the sign he finds honour and dishonour joined, the same token being venerated by some and received by others as absurd and monstrous. Chrysostom makes the rising a change of life, since when the sensual man becomes chaste and the covetous merciful a resurrection takes place, and notes that the sun is the more trying to weak sight the brighter it shines. Basil identifies the sign spoken against with the cross, Moses having made a brazen serpent and set it for a sign, and a sign betokening something marvellous.

Origen gives the plain sense of the fall and rising, a fall of unbelievers and a rising of believers, then unsettles it, since no one falls who was not before standing, so who stood, for whose fall he came? He answers from his own case, that while he stood in sin it was good for him to fall and die to sin; and he puts the contradiction of the sign not in believers, who know that all written of him is true, but in unbelievers, with whom everything written of him is a sign spoken against.

Calvin raises the difficulty that the less is blessed of the greater, and answers that the apostle means only the priestly blessing, Simeon having prayed as a private man for the advancement of Christ's kingdom as the Psalms prescribe; he uses the archer's mark for a general verdict, that the harmony of the world in opposing the gospel shows a natural enmity, men not conspiring so exactly without it, and ends on the revealing of thoughts, the lurking-places of human dissimulation being so deep that they stay hidden until Christ comes with his light. Gill offers for the sword the spear of scandal, the calumny Mary would meet for conceiving unmarried, then the sorrows that reached her from cradle to cross.

Barnes insists the word "again" is not in the Greek, so the same persons are not meant to fall and rise, while Ellicott allows that some may fall first and then, though sorely bruised, rise. Robertson sums the division in a borrowed line, that Judas despairs and Peter repents, one robber blasphemes and the other confesses. On the sword Lightfoot takes it for a prediction of martyrdom, thy soul meaning thy life, and cites Epiphanius, who allows that whether she died or was put to death she has a crown among the martyrs; Ellicott and Robertson identify the weapon as the long Thracian javelin, not the short Roman blade, and Robertson calls the clause a thorn among their roses.

Clarke takes the sign for a mark or butt to shoot at, a metaphor from archers, or else the ensign to which the Gentiles were to seek while the Jews rejected it; on the sword he leans to martyrdom but grants that respectable Greek writers use the figure for pungent sorrow.

debates.question: What is the sword that should pierce Mary's soul?

positions.view: A prediction of literal martyrdom; Epiphanius allows her a martyr's crown
Probably martyrdom, though the figure is used by Greek writers for pungent sorrow
Not martyrdom; no history tells of her being slain, and iron kills the body not the soul, so it is the grief of the passion
The calumny she would meet for conceiving unmarried, then the sorrows from cradle to cross
The word of God, sharper than the sharpest sword, and so a proof of her wisdom

debates.question: Do the same people fall and rise?

positions.view: No; the word "again" is not in the Greek
Some may fall first and then, though sorely bruised, rise
No one falls who was not before standing, so the question is who stood

outliers.claim: Alone reads the sword as the word of God rather than as sorrow or martyrdom, making the clause a testimony to Mary's wisdom instead of a prophecy of her suffering.

themes: And Joseph and his mother marvelled at those things which were spoken of him.
And Simeon blessed them, and said unto Mary his mother, Behold, this child is set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel; and for a sign which shall be spoken against;
(Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also,) that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed.

36.pericope_label: And there was one Anna, a prophetess, the daughter of Phanuel, of the tribe of Aser: she was of a great age, and had lived with an husband seven years from her virginity; And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day. And she coming in that instant gave thanks likewise unto the Lord, and spake of him to all them that looked for redemption in Jerusalem. And when they had performed all things according to the law of the Lord, they returned into Galilee, to their own city Nazareth. And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him.

schools.summary: Ambrose fits Anna into a series, since Simeon had prophesied, a wife had prophesied and a virgin had prophesied, and it was meet a widow should prophesy, that no condition should be wanting. Bede reads her mystically as the Church, widowed by her Husband's death, the eighty-four years being seven times twelve, seven for the course of this world and twelve for apostolic teaching; on the return to Nazareth he says Luke omitted what he knew Matthew had set forth, the flight into Egypt and the return after Herod's death, and observes that each Evangelist leaves out what he knows another will relate, so a careful reader finds the gaps only by comparison; and he distinguishes the terms of the growth, wisdom because in him dwelt all the fullness of the Godhead bodily, grace because it was given the man Christ Jesus to be from the first both perfect man and perfect God, the Word himself needing no strengthening.

Origen judges that long chastity and fasting made Anna worthy of prophecy, and accounts for the silence about her words by making Simeon the character of the law, whose name means obedience, and Anna the character of grace, which her name means, so that Christ came between them and Simeon departed with the law while Anna was sustained living on. Cyril joins the increase in wisdom to the increase in age, the divine nature unfolding its wisdom in proportion to bodily growth.

Theophylact observes that he might have come from the womb at full stature, but that this would have looked imaginary, and that wisdom displayed in infancy would have seemed a prodigy, whereas a gradual showing filled the world; he insists the strengthening in spirit is no receiving of wisdom, since what is most perfect at the beginning cannot become more perfect. The Greek Exposition puts the return to Nazareth before the descent into Egypt, the going up to Bethlehem having been only for the taxing, so that when it was done they went down to Nazareth of their own accord.

Robertson gives "prophetess" its old sense of a woman who interprets oracles and, reckoning the eighty-four as widowhood, reports Anna at a hundred and six; on the harmony he holds that the two Gospels supplement each other. Ellicott finds it remarkable that a woman should be a prophetess when no man was recognised as a prophet, and draws from her tribe that Aser, though carried into exile among the ten, was not altogether lost, its members keeping their genealogies; on the harmony he doubts that either Evangelist knew the other's narrative, each writing from what he heard, and says plainly that they cannot readily be harmonised. Lightfoot adds that she was a Galilean, which bears awkwardly on the saying that out of Galilee arises no prophet. Barnes agrees they returned but not immediately, defending the compression by the parallel of Paul, said to have come to Jerusalem on his conversion when three years had passed.

Clarke denies that Anna was a prophetess in the strict sense, taking her for a holy woman whose knowledge fitted her to instruct others, since prophesying is speaking to edification, and makes the eighty-four her whole age; on the return he supposes a journey to Galilee at once and a second return after Egypt.

Calvin leaves the reckoning of her years doubtful and presses another point, that two persons in whom the Spirit dwelt deserve more reverence than a multitude swelled with empty titles; he refuses outright the notion that the family settled at Bethlehem, calling it foolish to credit Joseph with an abode in a town where he could not find a lodging for a night.
Henry contrasts other children, who have foolishness bound in their hearts and show the corruption of their nature, where nothing but the grace of God was upon him.

debates.question: How old was Anna, and was she strictly a prophetess?

positions.view: Eighty-four in all, and not a prophetess in the strict sense but a holy woman who instructed others
A hundred and six, the eighty-four being her widowhood; a prophetess in the old sense of one who interprets oracles
The reckoning is doubtful and not the point
Remarkable that a woman should be a prophetess when no man was recognised as a prophet

debates.question: How does the return to Nazareth square with Matthew's flight into Egypt?

positions.view: Luke simply omitted what he knew Matthew had set forth
This verse stands before the descent into Egypt, the taxing being done
They returned, but not immediately; compression of this kind has a parallel in Paul
A return to Galilee at once and a second return after Egypt
Neither Evangelist knew the other; the two cannot readily be harmonised
The two Gospels supplement each other

outliers.claim: Notices that Anna, being of the tribe of Aser, was a Galilean, and so sets the chapter against the later proverb that out of Galilee arises no prophet.

And she was a widow of about fourscore and four years, which departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day.

41.pericope_label: Now his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover. And when he was twelve years old, they went up to Jerusalem after the custom of the feast. And when they had fulfilled the days, as they returned, the child Jesus tarried behind in Jerusalem; and Joseph and his mother knew not of it. But they, supposing him to have been in the company, went a day’s journey; and they sought him among their kinsfolk and acquaintance. And when they found him not, they turned back again to Jerusalem, seeking him.

schools.summary: Gill notes that Joseph was bound to the three feasts while the women were not, the passover of women being voluntary. Calvin sees no reason to wonder at the first day of the journey, and holds that the parents' later conduct shows the oversight was not indolence or carelessness.

Henry makes the yearly journey a lesson, since they were poor and the way long and had a son in the house able to teach them better than all the rabbins at Jerusalem, yet went up; and he turns the search into counsel, that whoever has lost his comforts in Christ should bethink himself where and when he lost them and return where he last had them.

Ellicott sets out the stages of Jewish childhood, the weaning at three, the Law at five, a direct responsibility at twelve and the phylacteries at thirteen, calling it an epoch of transition like our own confirmation, and adds that if the birth fell at the Paschal season the boy may have completed his thirteenth year during this feast; he denies that the child stayed behind by design, the words not implying it, and reconstructs the probable course, that he went as usual when the feast was over while his parents took for granted he had started with the other boys from Nazareth. Robertson agrees it was no disobedience but an intense interest in the temple services, an involuntary preoccupation that held him fast, describes the caravan, and quotes Plummer that the Nazareth company was so long it took a day to look through. Barnes offers three considerations for the oversight, that families and neighbours joined into a large company, that Jesus was probably with them while they prepared to start, and that part of the company may have gone ahead and been overtaken only at night. Lightfoot reports that the first day's journey from Jerusalem was thirty miles to Neapolis, while the spot shown to travellers as the place where the child was missed lies ten miles out, and leaves it there: you may believe those that show it as you think fit.

The Greek Exposition says he tarried secretly so that his parents should not hinder the discussion with the lawyers, and so that he might neither be kept away nor be disobedient. Epiphanius draws a doctrinal point from the age: at twelve and not at thirty Christ is already the astonishment of all men, so none may say the Spirit came at the baptism and made him the Christ, since from his childhood he acknowledged both the temple and his Father.

Bede supplies the custom that explains the lost day, that men and women travelled separately while the children went with either parent indifferently, so each thought in turn that the child was with the other. Ambrose makes the three days a sign that after three days of victorious suffering he who was believed dead should rise. The Gloss offers a figure of the three days, that the advent looked for by the patriarchs before the Law was not found, nor that sought by the prophets under the Law, but only that which the Gentiles seek under grace.

Origen presses where he was not: not among kinsfolk, since human relations could not comprehend the Son of God, nor among acquaintance, since he passes beyond all human knowledge; so seek him in the temple, among the masters who are in it, and seek with labour and sorrow, for many seek carelessly who never find him.

Clarke gives Bede's account of the separate companies and then turns on the parents: knowing what a treasure they possessed, how could they be so long without looking on it, and where were the bowels and tender solicitude of the mother? Let them answer who can.

debates.question: Did Jesus stay behind by design?

positions.view: Yes, secretly, so that his parents should not hinder the discussion, yet without disobedience
No; the words do not imply it, and his parents simply assumed he had started with the other boys
No disobedience, but an involuntary preoccupation with the temple services
The custom of separate companies explains it; each thought him with the other
It still looks inexcusable: where were the bowels and tender solicitude of the mother?
Three considerations clear them, chiefly the size of the travelling company
Their later conduct shows it was not indolence or carelessness

outliers.claim: Alone presses the oversight as a fault in the parents rather than explaining it away, asking where the mother's solicitude was and leaving the question for them to answer who can.

46.pericope_label: And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers. And when they saw him, they were amazed: and his mother said unto him, Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing. And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father’s business? And they understood not the saying which he spake unto them. And he went down with them, and came to Nazareth, and was subject unto them: but his mother kept all these sayings in her heart. And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man.

schools.summary: Lightfoot asks where in the temple this happened, listing three courts of judicature and a synagogue, and remarks that those who undertake to show the spot where the parents missed him may tell us which; he adds that it is hard to say what place a boy could be admitted to among the doctors. Robertson is flat on the crux, that the words mean in my Father's house and not about my Father's business, the pronoun being my and not our; they are the first words of Jesus preserved to us, a crisp idiom expressing amazement that his parents should not know there was one possible place in Jerusalem for him. He also adds Alford's note, that up to this time Joseph had been so called by the holy child himself and from this time never. Ellicott keeps the literal sense, the things that are my Father's, holding its vague width to cover the house as well, and calls it a prophecy of the consciousness of direct Sonship which the later life manifests; on the parents' failure to understand he grants that sceptical criticism finds here a contradiction with the Annunciation, answers that twelve years of ordinary childhood may have dulled the impressions and that the writer was conscious of no inconsistency, and sets the restraint of the record against the apocryphal gospels, where the child moulds sparrows of clay and claps them into flight and strikes a playmate dumb. Barnes mentions the house rendering but keeps the business.

Origen divides the posture, that because he was the Son of God he is in the midst of the doctors enlightening them, but because he was a little child he is found asking and not teaching, to set an example that wise children should hear their masters rather than teach them, though he asked not to learn but that in asking he might instruct; he notes too that Mary knew he was not Joseph's son and yet calls her husband his father, and asks why they sought him sorrowing, since they could not dread the loss of one they knew to be the Lord, answering that they sought as a man searches the Scriptures with pains, not supposing them to have erred but anxious to find the truth. Cyril answers the Eunomian heretics, that it is not the Word but the Word made flesh which is said to increase, the perfect nature being not enlarged but by degrees manifested, since the law of nature does not brook higher faculties than a man's age permits.

Chrysostom observes that the Lord did no miracle in his childhood, and that Luke records this one fact which made men wonder. The Greek Exposition has the mother make a mournful inquiry in everything like a mother, with confidence and humility and affection, and has the Lord set all at rest by correcting her word about his reputed father and manifesting his true one; it also finds three things in the subjection that follows, the love of God, honour to parents, and the preferring of God to parents. Theophylact says it more shortly than Cyril, that the showing forth of his wisdom is his increase.

Bede holds that he blames them not for seeking him as their son but compels them to raise their minds higher. Ambrose calls the subjection at Nazareth a mark not of weakness but of filial duty, since he was obedient to a handmaid and to his pretended father.
Calvin takes the doctrine from the answer, that whatever we owe to men must yield to the first table of the law, so we obey kings and parents only in subjection to God.

Clarke renders the words my Father's concerns but reports the house translation as defended by Grotius and Pearce and read by the Syriac, the later Persic and the Armenian, a child being looked for in his father's house.

debates.question: Is it "about my Father's business" or "in my Father's house"?

positions.view: In my Father's house, flatly; and the pronoun is my, not our
My Father's concerns, though the house rendering is defended by Grotius and Pearce and read by three versions
The literal "the things that are my Father's", whose vague width covers the house as well
The business, the work of God being always his work

debates.question: Why did the parents not understand?

positions.view: Twelve ordinary years may have dulled the earlier impressions; the writer saw no inconsistency
They blamed him as their son and had to be made to raise their minds higher
Whatever is owed to men yields to the first table of the law, which they had not yet grasped

outliers.claim: Turns the scene into a topographical and procedural problem, asking which of the temple's three courts or its synagogue is meant and what place a boy could have been admitted to among doctors who taught standing.
